business_model: Hardware sales (fitness trackers, speakers), one-time-purchase, low recurring-revenue component

historical_evidence.company: Consumer electronics company (formerly AliphCom) making wireless speakers and, from 2011, the UP line of fitness/wellness wearable trackers, backed by a roster of top-tier investors including Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, Khosla Ventures, and Kleiner Perkins.
historical_evidence.market: Fast-growing consumer wearables/fitness-tracking category as of 2014, but already showing signs of maturing competitive structure with a clear, better-resourced category leader.
historical_evidence.team: Experienced consumer-hardware team with a track record of shipping multiple product generations (speakers, then wearables) and raising from elite investors across several rounds.
historical_evidence.product: UP wearable fitness tracker line, competing directly against Fitbit and, by 2014, an entering Apple/Samsung on smartwatch-adjacent functionality — a crowded and rapidly evolving product category.
historical_evidence.execution: Raised $147M in September 2014 at a $3.2B valuation — a very large late-stage raise for a hardware company, suggesting either strong investor conviction or a need for significant additional capital to compete, or both.
historical_evidence.traction: REPAIRED (see benchmark_notes): NPD Group point-of-sale tracking data, reported by MobiHealthNews, covers the 52-week period from early January 2013 through early January 2014 and puts Fitbit at 68% of fitness-tracker retail unit sales, Jawbone UP at 19%, and Nike FuelBand at 10% — a real, dated, methodologically-labeled competitive-share statistic, though its measurement window ends roughly eight months before the September 2014 snapshot rather than coinciding with it. Looser, undated or vaguely-dated claims elsewhere in circulation (e.g., 'roughly 15%' or 'roughly 18%' for Jawbone 'in 2014') could not be traced to a source with a stated measurement period and have been excluded rather than used to corroborate a more dramatic gap.
historical_evidence.financial: No specific revenue or margin figures were found in the contemporaneous sources reviewed for this snapshot; the scale of the raise ($147M) alongside a distant #2 market position is itself a signal worth flagging for Burn Efficiency/Fundraising Readiness analysis.

future_outcome.outcome_summary: Jawbone raised additional capital through 2016 but was never able to close the competitive gap with Fitbit and other entrants; the company ceased operations and entered assignment-for-benefit-of-creditors liquidation in mid-2017, having raised roughly $930M in total venture funding.

benchmark_notes.why_included: Tests whether SIE correctly weighs a hard, contemporaneously-knowable competitive-share statistic against a very large, prestigious-investor-backed funding round — i.e., whether elite-investor participation alone inflates the Team/Fundraising-Readiness read despite a clearly unfavorable Market/Competitive-Intensity signal that was equally available at the time.
benchmark_notes.known_ambiguities: Reasonable analysts could differ on how much weight an 8-months-stale market-share statistic should carry versus the possibility of a comeback or a further-widened gap by the actual snapshot date — this is intentionally not an open-and-shut Very Weak case, since $147M from Sequoia/a16z/Khosla/Kleiner Perkins is a genuinely strong contemporaneous signal in the other direction.
benchmark_notes.evidence_limitations: No contemporaneous revenue, gross margin, or burn-rate figures were located for the 2014 snapshot specifically; Financial Health is expected to be evidence-thin for this record based on public sources alone.
benchmark_notes.evidence_repair_log: 2026-08-23: the original market_share_jawbone/market_share_fitbit facts (15%/38%) were sourced only to a 2017 CB Insights retrospective without a stated measurement period and without the required post-snapshot 'note' flag — a genuine hindsight-leakage risk flagged in the prior audit. Replaced with NPD Group data (via MobiHealthNews) carrying an explicit 52-week measurement window (Jan 2013-Jan 2014). TIER-QUESTIONABILITY FLAG (per audit Part 6, tier not changed): the replacement figures show a real but somewhat less extreme gap (19% vs. 68%, not 15% vs. 38%) and reflect a window ending ~8 months before the snapshot rather than September 2014 itself. The 'Weak' tier's evidentiary support is accordingly a bit softer than originally presented — a defensible reading of the funding trajectory alone ($147M from elite investors, up to a $3.2B valuation) would lean more toward 'Average' if the competitive-share evidence were excluded entirely. The tier is left unchanged pending separate adjudication, as instructed, but this softening should be weighed in that adjudication.
